GLM.content:
# GLM-5.3

Source: https://docs.z.ai/guides/llm/glm-5.3

[!TIP]

GLM-5.3 is now available to all GLM Coding Plan users, with 50% better coding performance! Subscribe now

## Overview

GLM-5.3 is Z.ai's latest flagship model, delivering comprehensive advancements in complex software engineering and agent capabilities. It uses the same base model as GLM-5.2, with all improvements driven by post-training. Compared with GLM-5.2, it delivers significantly stronger performance in complex programming and long-horizon tasks:

Stronger Coding Capability

GLM-5.3 delivers a significant improvement in coding capabilities, achieving a 50% performance gain over GLM-5.2 on Z.ai Code Bench. It also reaches state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance among open-source models on public benchmarks, including Terminal Bench 3.0 and Agents’ Last Exam (CLI).

Emergent Cyber Capability

As the scale of post-training continues to expand, the model’s cybersecurity capabilities have improved at a rate that exceeds expectations. GLM-5.3 achieves the best performance to date on the CyberGym vulnerability discovery benchmark. Moreover, the deeper it progresses along the vulnerability exploitation chain, the more pronounced its gains over GLM-5.2 become, with scores on vulnerability exploitation benchmarks exceeding twice those of GLM-5.2.

↗ Blog

## Feature Changes

GLM-5.3 currently supports text-only inputs, with a 1M-token context window and a maximum output length of 128K tokens. GLM-5.3 always operates with reasoning enabled and supports three reasoning effort levels:low, high, and max. Disabling reasoning is no longer supported. The reasoning parameters are described below:

Parameter | Values | Default | Description 
---|---|---|---
thinking.type | enabled | enabled | Supports reasoning only; disabling reasoning is not supported. 
reasoning_effort | low, high, max | max | low – Lightweight Reasoning; high – Enhanced Reasoning; max – Deep Reasoning 

[!NOTE]

Migration Notice: If your application currently uses
thinking.type: "disabled", please change it to enabled and set reasoning_effort to low before updating the model ID to glm-5.3. Otherwise, the request will fail.
For complex tasks such as coding, we recommend usingmax. An example is provided below:
{
  "model": "glm-5.3",
  "thinking": { "type": "enabled" },
  "reasoning_effort": "max"
}

For a detailed introduction to GLM-5.3’s advanced reasoning capabilities, please refer to the documentation: Deep Thinking

## How to Use

#### Model API

The supported protocols and endpoints are as follows:

Protocol | Base URL 
---|---
OpenAI Chat Completion Protocol | 	https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4 
OpenAI Response Protocol | 	https://api.z.ai/api/v1 
Anthropic Message Protocol | https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic 

↗ API Documentation：Learn how to call the API

[!NOTE]

If you have previously subscribed to a GLM Coding Plan, including an expired subscription, you can currently access the model API only through the OpenAI Chat Completion-compatible protocol. We will continue to improve and optimize this in upcoming iterations.

#### GLM Coding Plan

GLM-5.3 is now fully available, and you can use it with your preferred coding agents. Guide

The new GLM Coding Plan adopts a points-based quota system, providing transparent and predictable usage. Model calls made during off-peak hours, including all day on weekends, consume only 50% of the standard points. Subscribe now: Individual Plan、Team Plan.

## Capability Support

- Thinking Mode：Provides multiple thinking modes to accommodate different task requirements
- Streaming Messages：Supports real-time streaming responses for an enhanced user interaction experience
- Function Calling：Provides powerful tool-calling capabilities and supports integration with a wide range of external tools
- Context Caching：Uses an intelligent caching mechanism to optimize performance in long-context conversations
- Structured Output：Supports structured output formats such as JSON for seamless system integration

## Key Advancements

GLM-5.3 delivers significant improvements across complex software engineering, terminal operations, and a broader range of real-world Agent tasks.

#### Stronger Coding

For GLM-5.3, we pushed environment scaling toward tasks that look less like coding exercises and more like real units of expert work. The environments now cover a much broader range of production workflows, with tasks designed around how engineering and research work is actually carried out in practice. Some represent several days of work for an experienced engineer.

In an ML infrastructure task, for example, the model may be given the same working environment as an engineer, with access to compute clusters, storage systems, internal documentation, codebases, and experiment results. It must diagnose bottlenecks across the training stack, implement optimizations, run experiments, and deliver a measurable end-to-end speedup while preserving correctness. Training on environments at this level pushes the model toward taking ownership of substantial work end to end, rather than relying on users to decompose the problem and supervise each step.

As agent capability improves, much of the difficulty in scaling post-training moves from the model to the environment. A useful task environment has to be executable, verifiable, and close to real professional work — and we need many of them, not a handful of hand-built ones. To scale this process, we built pipelines that synthesize environments end to end, and for a subset of tasks, the RL reward signal as well. Research agents collect task patterns from real work and turn them into runnable long-horizon environments with multi-step dependencies and hidden state; a judge agent then attempts each task to verify that it is actually solvable. Verifiers are synthesized without access to the reference solution, while solver trajectories are used to discover and close reward shortcuts. A verifier that passes oracle, no-op, and unsolved-state checks produces a binary reward reliable enough to train on directly.

It carries over the RL strategies introduced in GLM-5.2, including SAO with compaction, which helps these gains hold on long-horizon tasks rather than only on short ones. The effect shows up across both coding and general agent tasks. GLM-5.3 improves from 4.6 to 28.3 on Terminal-Bench 3.0, from 46.2 to 66.9 on DeepSWE v1.1, and from 23.8 to 28.5 on Agents' Last Exam. These pipelines still require a meaningful amount of human-in-the-loop work; making environment generation and verification more autonomous is one of the next steps.

Beyond public benchmarks, we introduce Z.ai Code Bench, an in-house benchmark designed to evaluate coding agents under realistic user scenarios. It covers diverse task categories and places agents in complex local development environments. At different effort levels, we evaluate agents along two dimensions: end-to-end task completion rate and fine-grained checklist accuracy. As a private benchmark, Z.ai Code Bench also reduces the risk of contamination from public test sets and gives us a more faithful measure of real-world user experience.

As shown in the figure, GLM-5.3 improves both performance and token efficiency. It delivers markedly stronger agentic coding results than GLM-5.2 at every effort level while consuming fewer output tokens. At Max effort, GLM-5.3 reaches 34.5% at roughly 75K output tokens per task, compared with 23.4% at 96K for GLM-5.2. The same shift holds against closed models. At High effort, GLM-5.3 reaches 31.4% at around 50K output tokens, surpassing Claude Opus 4.8 at 29.5% with 120K. GLM-5.3 remains behind Claude Fable 5, which reaches 39.5% at Max effort.

#### Emergent Cyber Capability

As part of post-training, we introduced vulnerability discovery data and environments into the training mix. We expected this to make the model better at finding and reasoning about vulnerabilities. What surprised us was how quickly the capability continued to develop as training scaled. GLM-5.3 did not simply become better at identifying isolated flaws: it began to reason across multiple stages of exploitation, forming coherent plans for complete exploitation chains.

We evaluate GLM-5.3 across three benchmarks covering different stages of vulnerability analysis and exploitation.

We evaluate GLM-5.3 across three benchmarks covering different stages of vulnerability analysis and exploitation. On CyberGym, which starts from white-box source code and tests whether the model can identify and validate vulnerabilities by triggering faults, GLM-5.3 scores 84.5%, up from GLM-5.2's 77.2% — the best result on the benchmark, ahead of Mythos 5 (83.8%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (83.6%). On ExploitBench, which requires deeper reasoning about real vulnerabilities and their exploitation, GLM-5.3 reaches 54.4%, more than doubling GLM-5.2's 24.4%, while Mythos 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol score 78.0% and 76.5%, respectively. On ExploitGym, which measures how many exploitation tasks a model can complete under time-normalized budgets, GLM-5.3 completes 105 tasks within two hours and 130 within six hours, compared with 29 and 39 for GLM-5.2; budgets are normalized across models using per-model throughput figures, detailed in the footnotes. Mythos 5 remains well ahead at 181 and 247 tasks.

The pattern across the three is consistent: the further up the exploitation chain a benchmark sits, the larger the gain from GLM-5.2 — and also the wider the remaining gap to the closed frontier. Capability is growing fastest exactly where we are furthest behind.

We then tested whether these capabilities transfer beyond controlled benchmarks. Since GLM-5.2, we have been working with several security teams in China to run our models against real-world codebases. After expert review, screening, and deduplication, the model identified 2,436 vulnerabilities across 269 projects, including 1,097 medium-to-high severity issues. The findings span syste

GLM.content:
GLM-5.3-Flash/GLM-5.3-FlashX is the first native multimodal model in the GLM-5 series, delivering stronger intelligence than GLM-5.2 at an exceptionally low cost.

Highly Efficient Hybrid Architecture

GLM-5.3-Flash has 320B total parameters with 18B activated. As the first open-source frontier model to combine sparse and linear attention, it significantly cuts computation and serving costs while preserving long-context quality — reducing attention computation and KV cache by 3.01× and 4.44× versus GLM-5.3.

Native Multimodal Visual Coding

Visual capabilities are built into the coding loop: the model observes interfaces, rendered results, and interaction feedback to continuously test and improve its work. It coordinates tasks across code, browsers, and GUIs — from frontend and game development to Blender 3D scenes and real-world operation via BUA and CUA.

A Professional Work Partner Beyond Coding

Beyond coding, GLM-5.3-Flash supports professional workflows such as Office tasks, financial research, and document processing. It autonomously breaks down goals, invokes tools, and reviews outputs — from research and analysis to finished PPTX, PDF, DOCX, and XLSX deliverables.GLM-5.3-FlashX is now live, delivering inference speeds of 200 tokens/s for faster responses and a smoother experience.↗ blog

Parameter Settings：Text parameters are consistent with GLM-5.3, with support for a 1M-token context window.

Image Parameters：Add a content block with type: image_url to messages[].content[], and pass the image URL (recommended) or a Base64 Data URL through image_url.url. Multiple images can be added by including multiple image_url content blocks.

Recommended Settings： temperature: 1, top_p: 0.95, and reasoning_effort: max. thinking.type only supports enabled; we recommend setting thinking.clear_thinking: false. For streaming requests, we recommend enabling both stream: true and tool_stream: true.

GLM Coding Plan

Now fully available, GLM-5.3-Flash can be used with your preferred tools, with 3× the available quota compared with GLM-5.3. (GLM-5.3-FlashX is not yet available on the plan)

The new GLM Coding Plan adopts a points-based quota system with transparent usage limits. Model calls made during off-peak hours, including all day on weekends, consume only 50% of the standard points. Subscribe now: Personal Plan、Team Plan

Capabilities

Thinking Mode: Provides multiple thinking modes to address different task requirements. thinking.type only supports enabled; thinking cannot be disabled.

Streaming Output: Supports real-time streaming responses for an enhanced user interaction experience.

Function Calling: Provides powerful tool-calling capabilities and supports integration with a wide range of external tools.

Context Caching: Uses an intelligent caching mechanism to optimize long-conversation performance.

Structured Output: Supports structured output formats such as JSON for seamless system integration.

Visual Understanding: Native multimodal input supporting images, videos, and files.

Best Practices

Vision-Driven UI Coding: From Reference Assets to a Complete Application

GLM-5.3-Flash can directly transform screenshots, multiple page images, website URLs, or screen recordings into polished, functional applications. # China’s Z.ai ‘aggressively’ using looped transformer method to improve AI models

Company is first Chinese firm to disclose using emerging technique, which offers performance gains but also raises safety concerns

2-MIN READ2-MIN

Listen

Chinese artificial intelligence company Z.ai has credited an emerging technique – one that has drawn scrutiny from AI safety researchers – with helping its newly released flagship model achieve significant performance gains over its predecessor while improving computational efficiency.

The release marks the first time a Chinese AI company has disclosed using a “looped transformer” architecture in a major model, following recent reports that US giant OpenAI adopted the same method for its newest models.

In a blog post, Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, said it “aggressively” applied the technique over the past three months, enabling its GLM-5.4 model to match the performance of AI models two to four times its size.

GLM.title: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 is a 750B loop transformer | VentureBeat
GLM.description: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 aims to match models up to four times its size by running 28 layers twice ... GLM-5.4 is Z.ai's ... GLM-5.4 is available now through Z.ai's GLM Coding Plan, ZCode and Z.ai Chat.
GLM.content:
Featured

# Z.ai's GLM-5.4 aims to match models up to four times its size by running 28 layers twice

Z.ai's main evidence for the claim comes from a 30B test model, and early testers say the looped model is slow but useful for hunting bugs and security flaws.

GLM-5.4 is Z.ai's first flagship built on a Loop Transformer architecture, which reuses the same layers more than once instead of stacking new ones, so the model gets more depth and more computation per token without adding parameters. Thinking Machines Lab used a looped transformer in its Inkling 2 Mini model, which was released last week.

The GLM-5.4 model also adds vision and targets what Z.ai calls Generalized Coding, which applies code to engineering and design work such as mechanical design and 3D modeling, not only to software. GLM-5.4 follows GLM-5.3, which Z.ai released in August with advanced cyber capabilities.

GLM-5.4 is available now through Z.ai's GLM Coding Plan, ZCode and Z.ai Chat. API access is listed as coming soon, and Z.ai says open weights will follow after safety hardening, with no date given.

Z.ai has published a win-rate chart comparing GLM-5.4 with three other models, but without explaining the evaluation methodology. Its main controlled benchmark evidence comes from a separate test using a 30B model, and it acknowledges that GLM-5.4 can get caught in overly long reasoning loops.

## How GLM-5.4 works: 28 layers run twice instead of adding parameters

Z.ai describes large-scale software engineering, cybersecurity, 3D modeling and physical control as ultra-long-chain reasoning tasks, which require following multi-step causal chains while keeping global logical consistency.

"Stacking parameters and memorizing data cannot solve this," Z.ai said.

Conventional Transformers process each layer once per forward pass. GLM-5.4 instead sends intermediate representations through the same group of layers twice, increasing computational depth without adding parameters.

Researchers explored layer reuse in the 2018 Universal Transformer, although much of the subsequent work has focused on smaller models.

GLM-5.4 loops 28 layers of the GLM-5 base for two iterations at the 750B scale, adapted from an already pre-trained model through continued training.

Looping carries costs of its own, so Z.ai made three architectural changes to balance performance against deployment cost.

Gated progressive updates. Repeatedly updating the model's internal representations can cause instability. Z.ai says GLM-5.4 uses per-token gates to control how much each iteration changes them.

Z.ai reports that after training the first pass builds global context and writes conservatively. The second pass opens the gates to write full updates. The gates also adjust step size by token difficulty, so harder tokens get more aggressive first-pass writes.

Hybrid KV cache. Rather than maintaining a complete KV cache for each iteration, GLM-5.4 reuses the first pass's sparse KV cache and limits additional storage to a sliding window for the second pass.

Sparse attention index reuse. The second loop reuses the attention indices from the first loop's indexer, which avoids a second indexing pass. Z.ai's experiments show this performs nearly identically to recomputing indices on every pass.

## Early tests show gains on a 30B model, but questions remain about GLM-5.4's performance

Z.ai describes GLM-5.4 as reaching intelligence levels comparable to 2T-3T parameter models, but does not explain how it arrived at that comparison.

Its main controlled evidence is a 30B test model, where the looped version used about 10% more training compute than a non-looped baseline of the same size. Z.ai reports the largest improvements in math, scientific reasoning and long-context tasks, along with shorter average outputs, by about 15% on MMLU-Pro and 12% on GPQA-Diamond. Those results were measured on the smaller test model, not GLM-5.4 itself.

## Community reactions: Testers praise bug-finding and security work but flag speed and a gap to Opus 5.5

Developers who tried GLM-5.4 in its first hours report strengths in code review and security testing, and criticism over speed and rivals' lead.

In a post on X, AICodeKing placed GLM-5.4 seventh on his KingBench 4 coding benchmark. At maximum reasoning effort, GLM-5.4 took 431 minutes to complete the tests, compared with 109 minutes for Google's Gemini 4 Neon. It required 1,128 steps versus 244 for Neon.

"I wouldn't recommend you to just use this model but keeping it as a reviewer for work and making it work on more complex architecture or searching for bugs, security vulnerabilities is really worth it imo,” AICodeKing wrote.

Migel Tissera tested GLM-5.4 as a black-box attacker against a private lab environment and said it successfully completed a multistep remote code execution chain, according to his post on X.

Not every tester was persuaded.

"Sorry but GLM 5.4 is nowhere near Opus 5.5 not a single Open model is right now,” Loktar wrote on X.

Darek Gusto welcomed the built-in vision and the extra quota but noted the missing coding benchmark scores. In a post on X, Gusto wrote: "After GLM 5.4 dropped, I wanted my jaw to drop too, and it kinda did... when I realized that even in the blog there are no coding benchmarks."

A poster on Reddit r/LocalLLaMA was particularly critical of the model for any use case outside of coding. The poster also complained that the model spends half of its chain of thought wasting tokens on reasoning about whether something is OK.

## Pricing, Coding Plan and availability

GLM-5.4 is now available through the GLM Coding Plan, ZCode and Z.ai Chat. For users on weekly quota plans, Z.ai says GLM-5.4's quota is 1.5 times that of GLM-5.3.

According to Z.ai's developer documentation, GLM-5.4 accepts text, image, video and file inputs and returns text, with a 1M-token context window and a maximum output of 128K tokens. Its predecessor GLM-5.3 accepts text only. The launch post gives no vision benchmark scores.

General API pricing has not been announced. Z.ai says API access is coming soon, after it completes a security assessment. For reference, Z.ai's docs list GLM-5.3 at $1.40 per million input tokens, 26 cents for cached input and $4.40 per million output tokens. GLM-5.4 is not on that page.

Z.ai has not given a date for open weights or said which license they will carry.

"We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening," the company stated.

Kimi.description: Moonshot (Kimi) Moonshot AI provides an OpenAI-compatible API for its Kimi models — the Kimi K3 and K2 thinking models and the Moonshot v1 generation models. ... - Kimi K3 — flagship thinking model, 1M context ... - Kimi K2 — thinking models, 256k context...
Kimi.content:
# Moonshot (Kimi)

Moonshot AI provides an OpenAI-compatible API for its Kimi models — the Kimi K3 and K2 thinking models and the Moonshot v1 generation models. The Moonshot provider extends the OpenAI provider, so all of its options are supported.

## Setup

- Get an API key from the Kimi (Moonshot) platform.
- Set theMOONSHOT_API_KEY environment variable or specify apiKey in your config.

Kimi K3 requires a successful account top-up of at least $1; see the access requirements.
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3

Bothmoonshot:<model> and moonshot:chat:<model> resolve to the chat completions endpoint. If you omit the model, the provider defaults to kimi-k3.

## Available Models

Moonshot's lineup rotates over time — call the list models API (GET https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/models) for the live set. As of writing:

- Kimi K3 — flagship thinking model, 1M context:kimi-k3 (released July 2026). Always-on reasoning, native image and video understanding, and a top-level reasoning_effort control (see below).
- Kimi K2 — thinking models, 256k context:kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.5, kimi-k2.7-code, kimi-k2.7-code-highspeed. These reason before answering and emit a separate reasoning stream (see below).
- Moonshot v1 — legacy generation models:moonshot-v1-8k, moonshot-v1-32k, moonshot-v1-128k (context-length variants) and the vision variants moonshot-v1-8k-vision-preview / moonshot-v1-32k-vision-preview / moonshot-v1-128k-vision-preview; existing accounts may also see the auto-router moonshot-v1-auto in the list-models API. The moonshot-v1 series and kimi-k2.5 are closed to newly registered users and sunset platform-wide on August 31, 2026.

The olderkimi-k2-0711-preview, kimi-k2-0905-preview, kimi-k2-turbo-preview, kimi-k2-thinking, kimi-k2-thinking-turbo, and kimi-latest ids were discontinued in 2026 — Moonshot recommends migrating to kimi-k3.

## Configuration
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3 # flagship thinking model — leave sampling params unset
  - id: moonshot:moonshot-v1-8k # legacy generation model — accepts arbitrary sampling
    config:
      temperature: 0.2
      max_tokens: 1024

### Configuration Options

The provider accepts every option the OpenAI provider supports. Commonly used:

- temperature, max_tokens, top_p, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty
- stream
- response_format (JSON mode), tools / tool_choice (function calling)
- showThinking — set to false to drop a thinking model's reasoning from the graded output (default true)
- cost, inputCost, outputCost, cacheReadCost — Moonshot ships no built-in price table, so set these to track cost. Every override is in USD per token. Moonshot's official pricing page publishes rates in USD per 1 million tokens, so divide each published rate by 1,000,000 before configuring it. inputCost/outputCost take precedence over the flat cost; cacheReadCost prices cached prompt tokens.

For example, these illustrative per-million rates convert to per-token overrides. Check the official pricing page for the current rates for your model before using them.
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3
    config:
      inputCost: 0.000003 # $3.00 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      cacheReadCost: 0.0000003 # $0.30 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      outputCost: 0.000015 # $15.00 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k2.6
    config:
      inputCost: 0.00000095 # $0.95 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      cacheReadCost: 0.00000016 # $0.16 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      outputCost: 0.000004 # $4.00 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000

Any other parameter supported by the OpenAI provider is forwarded as-is.

## Kimi thinking models

Thekimi-k3 and kimi-k2.x models are reasoning models and behave differently from the moonshot-v1 family:

- Fixed sampling parameters. Kimi pinstemperature (1.0 with thinking on), top_p, n, and the penalties to fixed values and returns a 400 ("invalid temperature: only 1 is allowed for this model") for any other value. The provider therefore does not send promptfoo's default temperature/max_tokens for kimi-* models — leave them unset (recommended) or set temperature: 1. The moonshot-v1 models accept arbitrary sampling values.
- Reasoning output. Kimi returns a separatereasoning_content stream that promptfoo surfaces with a Thinking: … prefix. Set showThinking: false when you assert on structured output (for example is-json) so the reasoning doesn't contaminate the parsed result.
- Token budget. Reasoning tokens count against the output budget. When you leave the token limit unset the provider lets Moonshot apply its server default (32k for K2.x, 131k for K3); if you set one, leave generous headroom for the answer. Moonshot's canonical field ismax_completion_tokens (max_tokens is a deprecated alias) — the provider sends max_completion_tokens for kimi-* models whichever of the two you configure.
- Controlling thinking. The two generations use different, mutually exclusive controls:
- kimi-k3 is always thinking and accepts a top-level reasoning_effort field, which the provider forwards from config.reasoning_effort. Supported values are low, high, and max (the default). Do not send the K2.x thinking parameter to K3 — the API rejects it.
- kimi-k2.6 and kimi-k2.5 support thinking: { type: disabled } (pass it via config.passthrough); kimi-k2.7-code is always thinking. The thinking parameter is K2.x-only.
- Settingconfig.reasoning_effort on a non-K3 model is a configuration error and the provider fails fast with a clear message instead of sending it.

providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3
    config:
      showThinking: false
      reasoning_effort: max # optional: low, high, or max (default)
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k2.6
    config:
      passthrough:
        thinking: { type: disabled } # K2.x only: turn reasoning off

See the Kimi K3 quickstart and Using Thinking Models for the full behavior matrix.

## Vision

The vision models (moonshot-v1-*-vision-preview) and the multimodal Kimi models (kimi-k3, kimi-k2.5, kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.7-code, kimi-k2.7-code-highspeed) accept base64-encoded image input using the standard OpenAI image_url content format. Moonshot does not accept remote image URLs — embed images as data: URIs or reference files uploaded to the Kimi platform as ms://<file-id>. Video input is supported by kimi-k3, kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.7-code, and kimi-k2.7-code-highspeed, referenced the same way after uploading via the files API. See Use the Kimi Vision Model.

## Example Usage
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3
  - id: openai:gpt-4o-mini

prompts:
  - 'Summarize the following in one sentence: {{text}}'

tests:
  - vars:
      text: 'Promptfoo is an open-source tool for testing and evaluating LLM apps.'

A runnable comparison lives in examples/provider-moonshot.

## API Details

- Base URL:https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 (global). China-mainland keys use https://api.moonshot.cn/v1 — point at it with apiBaseUrl, since the global and China platforms issue region-locked keys.
- OpenAI-compatible chat completions API.
- Full API documentation.

## See Also

- OpenAI Provider — compatible configuration options
- Kimi model list and pricing

# Moonshot AI / Kimi

Use Moonshot AI's Kimi models throughMoonshotAIProvider and the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. The provider prefix is moonshotai:.

The Kimi K3.1 Pro API guide coverskimi-k3.1-pro and kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed.
Use thinking='low', thinking='high', or thinking='max'
to select a documented reasoning effort, or omit thinking to use the provider's default.

## Install

Install Pydantic AI with the OpenAI SDK used by this integration:
pip/uv-add "pydantic-ai-slim[openai]"

## Configuration

Create an API key in the Moonshot Console.

You can set theMOONSHOTAI_API_KEY environment variable and use MoonshotAIProvider by name:
from pydantic_ai import Agent

agent = Agent('moonshotai:kimi-k3.1-pro')
...

Or initialise the model and provider directly:
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.models.openai import OpenAIChatModel
from pydantic_ai.providers.moonshotai import MoonshotAIProvider

model = OpenAIChatModel(
    'kimi-k3.1-pro',
    provider=MoonshotAIProvider(api_key='your-moonshot-api-key'),
)
agent = Agent(model)
...

### Custom base URL

MoonshotAIProvider uses https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 by default. To use the Chinese endpoint,
set MOONSHOTAI_BASE_URL and an API key from the Chinese console:
export MOONSHOTAI_API_KEY="your-moonshot-api-key"
export MOONSHOTAI_BASE_URL="https://api.moonshot.cn/v1"

You can then use the model-string configuration shown above.

Alternatively, passbase_url='https://api.moonshot.cn/v1' to
MoonshotAIProvider.
An explicit base_url overrides MOONSHOTAI_BASE_URL.

## Thinking

Kimi K2.5, K2.6, K2.7 Code and K3 reason by default. The unifiedthinking setting maps onto Moonshot's request fields:

- thinking=False turns thinking off on Kimi K2.5 and K2.6 by sending thinking={'type': 'disabled'}. Kimi K3 can't turn thinking off, so it reasons at its lowest effort, reasoning_effort='low'. Kimi K2.7 Code can't turn thinking off either and has no effort setting, so thinking=False sends nothing.
- thinking=True and the effort levels are sent as reasoning_effort (True as 'medium'). 'max' is sent as 'max' on Kimi K3, K2.6 and K2.7, and as 'xhigh' on the other Kimi models.

Review historical Kimi Open Platform feature releases, model launches, product improvements, and issue fixes.

This page is updated periodically with Kimi Open Platform product updates and related documentation changes.

🔒 Privacy Policy update

Updated the Privacy Policy with revised disclosures on how we collect, use, and share personal information, and the rights and choices available to users.

📦 Batch API now supports Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3

The Batch API now supports the kimi-k3.1-pro and kimi-k3 models (previously limited to kimi-k2.7-code and kimi-k2.6), available on both the CN and Global platforms. Batch inference is still priced at 60% of standard rates; batch jobs on kimi-k3.1-pro and kimi-k3 are also charged Cache Write fees, and because batch requests are processed asynchronously and concurrently, cache hits are provided on a best-effort basis. See the Batch API Guide and BatchJob Pricing.

Account usage is now deducted at a uniform ratio of 50% cash and 50% vouchers. When either balance is depleted, all subsequent usage is deducted from the remaining balance type. Users with signed contracts follow their contract terms and continue to prioritize voucher usage — they are not affected.

The kimi-k2.5 and all moonshot-v1 series models (including -vision-preview and moonshot-v1-auto) were retired across all platforms. Calls to these models now return a 404 “model not found” error. Please migrate to Kimi K3.

Files API updates: newly generated file IDs now carry the file_ prefix; improved parsing of complex content such as tables and formulas; images are no longer OCR’d for text extraction (for image understanding, upload images with purpose=image; see Use Vision Models); files uploaded with the same name as an existing file are automatically renamed by the server.

🚀 Kimi K3 available on the Open Platform API

Kimi K3 — our flagship model for long-horizon coding and end-to-end knowledge work — is now available through the Open Platform API, with a 1M token context and leading overall intelligence. See the Kimi K3 Quickstart. At the same time, kimi-k2.5 and the moonshot-v1 series are no longer offered to newly registered users; the Global edition added email verification-code sign-up/login and email & Google account binding management. The account overview now shows current-day spending, and the platform Terms of Service have been updated.

Added organization-level API IP allowlists for finer enterprise security control.

Released Kimi K2.7 Code through the Open Platform API, followed by a HighSpeed variant; custom top-up amounts are now supported.

The kimi-k2 series (including kimi-k2-0905-preview, kimi-k2-0711-preview, kimi-k2-turbo-preview, kimi-k2-thinking, and kimi-k2-thinking-turbo) was retired and is no longer maintained or supported. Please migrate to Kimi K3.

Added automatic balance top-up and top-up amount configuration.

The Batch API is now open to all users for lower-cost large-scale asynchronous inference — see Use the Batch API.

Released Kimi K2.6 through the Open Platform API.

Released Kimi K2.5 through the Open Platform API; discontinued kimi-latest.

Added organization verification, member invitations, and multi-account organization support to the Global Open Platform.

Released Kimi K2 Thinking and its Turbo variant, increased default TPM limits across tiers, and reduced Kimi Turbo prices; discontinued kimi-thinking-preview.

Updated Kimi CLI and K2 quickstart documentation, ended the Kimi Turbo half-price promotion, refreshed K2VV and sales information, and retired manual Context Cache list views.

Launched the kimi-k2-0905-preview model.

Released the Kimi K2 high-speed model kimi-k2-turbo-preview and launched the Global Open Platform developer forum.

Released the Kimi K2 model kimi-k2-0711-preview; launched Kimi Playground with streaming output and third-party and ModelScope MCP server configuration; added API access to Formula Tools and improved Global top-up and voucher terms.

Released the Kimi Thinking model kimi-thinking-preview; launched the Global edition of Kimi Open Platform.

Reduced model product pricing; added support for inviting and managing organization members; fixed an issue where the cursor could not move in the name field when creating a project.

Launched the kimi-latest model; added support for exporting organization monthly bills; fixed project rate limit display issues; added support for project daily and monthly spending alerts.

Launched the moonshot-v1-vision-preview model; added support for organization project management; added support for overseas phone number registration and login.

Optimized the resource management list copy interaction to use hover and click; optimized resource list sorting by upload time, from newest to oldest; added support for multiple accounts under one verified business entity; fixed an invoice cancellation failure issue.

Context Caching is now available to all users, and cache renewal no longer charges the creation fee; added terms and agreements content to the documentation center; fixed frontend flickering after successful payment, invoice cancellation failures, and issues with editing and deleting API Keys.

Added frontend support for file resource management; split phone number rebinding into two frontend verification steps; added verification-code purpose descriptions to SMS messages; fixed an issue where the invoiceable amount was displayed incorrectly and an invoice issuance failure caused by spaces in the tax identification number; added bank transfer processing time display for business verification; added documentation for automatic disconnection and reconnection handling; launched web search.

Launched moonshot-v1-auto; added support for custom account balance alerts; added support for phone number rebinding; added support for account password login; reduced Cache storage costs; published the MoonPalace user guide; released the Kimi Enterprise API; added tier level display to basic user information.

Launched the Context Caching public beta and gradually expanded it, adding practice blogs and the developer community; released MoonPalace, the Kimi API debugging tool, along with user spending analysis and organization verification capabilities.

Optimized the API Key count limit; published the first Context Caching practice blog for Kimi API Assistant; published the “Affordable Long-Text Processing” blog; added support for voucher validity periods.

Launched the Blog space; added Dark Mode support for Open Platform; launched invoice management.

Launched Tool Calling; launched identity verification; added support for the balance monitoring API.

#### Model Capabilities

# Best Practices Guide

This guide collects the practices that get the best results from Grok text and reasoning models on the xAI API. It covers which API to use, how to carry reasoning across turns, how to lower cost with prompt caching, how to configure requests, and how to run evaluations.

Start with these settings:

Setting | Recommendation 
---|---
API | Use the Responses API. Chat Completions is deprecated. 
Multi-turn history | Send the encrypted reasoning content back to the API with every turn. 
Prompt caching | Give each conversation its own prompt_cache_key, and only append to the conversation. 
Reasoning effort | Set it explicitly on every request, and record it with every result. 
Streaming and timeouts | Prefer streaming. Allow at least 900 seconds per request, and 1800 seconds or more for long-running evals. 
Output length | Set max_output_tokens above your longest expected answer, or leave it at its 128,000-token default. 
Sampling | Set temperature to 0.7 and top_p to 0.95, and don't stray far from them. 

## Use the Responses API

Use the Responses API (POST /v1/responses) with Grok reasoning models. The Chat Completions API is deprecated, and it has no field for the model's encrypted reasoning, so every multi-turn or tool-calling conversation sent through it discards the model's earlier thinking. New capabilities also arrive on the Responses API first.

If your code already uses Chat Completions, the comparison guide maps each parameter and response field to its Responses API equivalent.

Chat Completions is offered only as a legacy endpoint. Results from it understate what Grok reasoning models can do, especially across multiple turns and tool calls.

## Send encrypted reasoning back with every turn

Grok reasoning models think before they answer. The Responses API returns that reasoning as an encryptedreasoning item in the response's output array, alongside the message and any function calls. When you send these items back unchanged in the next request's input, the model stays aware of its earlier reasoning traces. This drastically improves performance on multi-turn conversations and agent loops, where each step builds on decisions the model already reasoned through.

There are two ways to keep reasoning in the conversation:

- Chain requests withprevious_response_id while store is on (the default). SpaceXAI stores the reasoning with the response and restores it for you.
- Manage the history yourself withstore: false. Request the reasoning with include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"] and append every output item to the next request's input. Each request is then self-contained and carries the full conversation, which you can log and replay.

grok-4.7 returns reasoning.encrypted_content on every Responses API response, whether or not include lists it. Your code still has to send it back. See Adding encrypted thinking content for the full reference.

The following loop runs a scripted multi-turn conversation. It streams each turn, carries the encrypted reasoning forward, reuses oneprompt_cache_key for the whole conversation, and prints how many input tokens were served from the cache:
import os
import uuid

import httpx
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.getenv("XAI_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://api.x.ai/v1",
    timeout=httpx.Timeout(900.0),
)

conversation_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
history = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a careful analyst. Answer concisely."}]

turns = [
    "A train leaves at 9:40 and arrives at 13:05. How long is the trip?",
    "The return trip is 20% faster. When does it arrive if it leaves at 15:00?",
]

for turn in turns:
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": turn})
    stream = client.responses.create(
        model="grok-4.7",
        input=history,
        reasoning={"effort": "high"},
        temperature=0.7,
        top_p=0.95,
        include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
        store=False,
        stream=True,
        extra_body={"prompt_cache_key": conversation_id},
    )
    response = None
    for event in stream:
        if event.type == "response.output_text.delta":
            print(event.delta, end="", flush=True)
        elif event.type in ("response.completed", "response.incomplete"):
            response = event.response
    print()
    # Append every output item, including reasoning items with encrypted_content.
    history.extend(response.output)
    print(f"Cached tokens: {response.usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens}")
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
    apiKey: process.env.XAI_API_KEY,
    baseURL: "https://api.x.ai/v1",
    timeout: 900000,
});

const conversationId = randomUUID();
const history = [
    { role: "system", content: "You are a careful analyst. Answer concisely." },
];

const turns = [
    "A train leaves at 9:40 and arrives at 13:05. How long is the trip?",
    "The return trip is 20% faster. When does it arrive if it leaves at 15:00?",
];

for (const turn of turns) {
    history.push({ role: "user", content: turn });
    const stream = await client.responses.create({
        model: "grok-4.7",
        input: history,
        reasoning: { effort: "high" },
        temperature: 0.7,
        top_p: 0.95,
        include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
        store: false,
        stream: true,
        prompt_cache_key: conversationId,
    });
    let response;
    for await (const event of stream) {
        if (event.type === "response.output_text.delta") {
            process.stdout.write(event.delta);
        } else if (event.type === "response.completed" || event.type === "response.incomplete") {
            response = event.response;
        }
    }
    console.log();
    // Append every output item, including reasoning items with encrypted_content.
    history.push(...response.output);
    console.log(`Cached tokens: ${response.usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens}`);
}
import os
import uuid

from xai_sdk import Client
from xai_sdk.chat import system, user

conversation_id = str(uuid.uuid4())

client = Client(
    api_key=os.getenv("XAI_API_KEY"),
    timeout=900,
    # Routes every turn of this conversation to the same server for cache reuse.
    metadata=(("x-grok-conv-id", conversation_id),),
)

chat = client.chat.create(
    model="grok-4.7",
    reasoning_effort="high",
    temperature=0.7,
    top_p=0.95,
    store_messages=False,
    use_encrypted_content=True,
)
chat.append(system("You are a careful analyst. Answer concisely."))

turns = [
    "A train leaves at 9:40 and arrives at 13:05. How long is the trip?",
    "The return trip is 20% faster. When does it arrive if it leaves at 15:00?",
]

for turn in turns:
    chat.append(user(turn))
    for response, chunk in chat.stream():
        print(chunk.content, end="", flush=True)
    print()
    # Appending the response also appends its encrypted reasoning.
    chat.append(response)
    print(f"Cached tokens: {response.usage.cached_prompt_text_tokens}")

The Vercel AI SDK carries encrypted reasoning automatically when you chain requests withpreviousResponseId; see Reasoning.

### Keep reasoning in agent loops

Tool-calling workloads need the same treatment. When the model calls a function, its reasoning item arrives in the sameoutput array as the function_call. Append the whole array, then your function_call_output items, so the model resumes with its plan intact when it reads the tool result:

Python (OpenAI)
import json

# client, tools, task_prompt, run_tool, and conversation_id come from your code.
def stream_turn(input_items):
    stream = client.responses.create(
        model="grok-4.7",
        input=input_items,
        tools=tools,
        reasoning={"effort": "high"},
        temperature=0.7,
        top_p=0.95,
        include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
        store=False,
        stream=True,
        extra_body={"prompt_cache_key": conversation_id},
    )
    for event in stream:
        if event.type in ("response.completed", "response.incomplete"):
            return event.response

input_items = [{"role": "user", "content": task_prompt}]

while True:
    response = stream_turn(input_items)
    # Reasoning, messages, and function calls all go back in order.
    input_items.extend(response.output)

    calls = [item for item in response.output if item.type == "function_call"]
    if not calls:
        break

    for call in calls:
        result = run_tool(call.name, json.loads(call.arguments))
        input_items.append({
            "type": "function_call_output",
            "call_id": call.call_id,
            "output": json.dumps(result),
        })

print(response.output_text)

Code drops reasoning most often in one of these ways:

- It extractsoutput_text and appends it as a plain assistant message, discarding the reasoning and function call items around it.
- It edits, reorders, or filters output items before sending them back. Pass them back exactly as received.
- It rebuilds the conversation from a transcript in a different format, such as a Chat Completionsmessages array, between turns.

Troubleshooting Reasoning shows how to check your requests for each of these and how to fix them.

For long agent loops, WebSocket mode reduces per-turn latency, and context compaction keeps long conversations within the context window.

## Use prompt caching to lower cost

The xAI API caches prompts automatically, and cached input tokens are billed at a lower rate than regular input tokens; see Pricing for each model's cached token price. The cache matches your input from the start: when a request begins with exactly the same items as an earlier request, that matching prefix is served from the cache, and only the new items are processed. Multi-turn conversations and agent loops benefit the most, because each turn resends everything before it.

#### Use Grok Bot

# Grok Bot for Mobile

Use Grok Bot on iPhone or Android to start work, answer questions, approve steps, and review results away from your desk.

The mobile app connects to the same Bots, conversations, routines, connectors, and shared cloud computer as the desktop app. Work continues in the cloud when the app is closed.

## Requirements

- iPhone with iOS 18 or later, or a phone with Android 9 or later
- An eligible plan: Premium, Super, or Ultra on The X Subscription, for an individual or a team seat. On a legacy Cursor plan, every paid individual plan and Cursor Teams include Grok Bot, and you can also link an individual SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, SuperGrok Heavy, or X Premium+ subscription. See Grok Bot on The X Subscription and Plans and billing.
- Internet connection

The iOS app also runs on iPad (iPadOS 18 or later).

Download Grok Bot from the App Store on iPhone or Google Play on Android.

## Sign in and set up

- Open Grok Bot.
- On iPhone, choose Continue with Google, Sign in with Apple, or Continue with email. If you're signed in to the X app or the Grok app on the same iPhone, Grok Bot can offer Continue as that account instead; choose Other options to see the rest. On Android, choose Log In or Sign Up and complete sign-in in the browser.
- Use the same account you use on desktop or web. If your account asks for a code from an authenticator app, enter it on the Enter your verification code screen, or choose Use the browser instead.
- Return to the app. If your access comes from a SuperGrok or X Premium+ subscription, choose Link Grok Account when the access screen asks, finish signing in to Grok in the browser, then choose Finished Linking? Refresh My Status. A link made on desktop or the web also works on the phone with the same Cursor account.

New users can complete the first-run tour, choose a first Bot, and wait while the shared computer is set up. Existing users go directly to their synced Bot list.

Enable notifications if you want to know when a Bot has a result, question, or approval request. While you use the desktop app on macOS or Windows, notifications from Bots you own go to the desktop instead; see Control notifications for when your phone is still notified.

There is no setting that keeps your phone quiet only while the desktop app is open. To stop alerts for one Bot, tap the Bot's name at the top of its chat and turn off Notifications; the note there is Get notified when this Bot finishes or is waiting for you. Off means that Bot does not notify you, including on your phone. On desktop, ask the Bot to turn its notifications off. To stop phone alerts for every Bot, open Settings on the phone and turn off Notifications. If the phone says Notifications are off, choose Open Settings and allow notifications for Grok Bot there only if you want them back.

## Access and subscriptions

Grok Bot access carries into mobile when you sign in with the same Cursor account. This includes:

- Premium, Super, or Ultra on The X Subscription, including team seats
- Legacy Cursor Ultra, Cursor Pro+, or Cursor Pro
- Legacy Cursor Teams (self-serve) seats
- SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, or SuperGrok Heavy account links
- X Premium+ account links

You should not buy a second subscription through Apple or Google Play in these cases. You can still upgrade within your plans, such as Pro+ to Ultra. A Cursor plan and a SuperGrok or X Premium+ link do not add together; Grok Bot uses whichever one grants more weekly usage. Your phone and desktop share the same usage on your Cursor account.

### Subscribe from the phone

If your Cursor account doesn't already include Grok Bot, subscribe from the mobile app:

- Open Grok Bot on your phone.
- Choose a plan on the paywall screen.
- Complete the in-app purchase through the App Store on iOS or Google Play on Android.

Only monthly individual plans are available through the mobile app. For yearly billing, Teams, or Enterprise plans, subscribe on cursor.com. If you subscribed in the app and want on-demand usage, enable it on the web.

### Manage or cancel a phone subscription

The store you bought through handles the subscription, including store free trials (intro offers). Cursor can't cancel an in-app plan or refund it for you.

- iOS: Apple handles in-app subscriptions. Cancel or change the plan in Apple ID → Subscriptions before a trial ends if you do not want it to convert to a paid subscription. For Apple billing questions and refunds, use Apple's subscription support.
- Android: Google Play handles in-app subscriptions. Cancel or change the plan in the Google Play app under Payments & subscriptions → Subscriptions. For Google Play billing questions and refunds, use Google Play's refund support. Android has no in-app trial. A Google Play subscription belongs to the Grok Bot account that bought it. If it was bought while you were signed in to a different Grok Bot account, changing the plan from the app fails with a general error and nothing is charged. Sign in to the account that owns the subscription to change the plan, or let it end and subscribe again from the account you want to use.

The Grok Bot usage-credit trial claimed on web or desktop is separate; see Is there a free trial?.

### Use a usage limit reset

A usage limit reset brings your weekly usage back to 0% right away, without waiting for your regular weekly reset. Resets you have are listed under Usage limit resets in Settings > Usage, with the date each one expires. Tap Usage limit reset, then Confirm. After you use one, you have to wait before you can use another.

When you reach your weekly usage limit, the warning above the message box also offers Use reset. It isn't offered before you reach the limit, because using a reset early gives up the usage you have left that week.

If you have no resets and can refer friends, Usage limit resets shows No resets available. Tap it to refer a friend for a free usage reset.

## Message a Bot

From a conversation, you can:

- Send text
- Dictate a message with Start dictation
- Start a voice chat with Start voice chat
- Play a voice memo a Bot sent
- Take or attach a photo
- Choose an image or file
- Mention another Bot or@everyone in a group
- Reply in a thread
- React to a message

Drafts are saved per conversation when you navigate away.

Touch and hold a message and choose Select Text to select its text in place. Adjust the selection, then choose Add to Chat to quote it in your reply, or copy it.

To send something from another app, use the system share sheet and choose Grok Bot. You can share a photo, file, link, or text on iPhone, and text, photos, videos, audio, or PDFs on Android. Grok Bot sends it without leaving the app you're in: your primary Bot, if you have one, starts in To:, or pick another Bot from the list or search for one. Optionally Add a note, then choose Send. If the share can't be sent from there, choose Open in Grok Bot to finish in the app.

Choose Start voice chat when the composer is empty to talk with the Bot live. While you are on the line, a Voice chat control stays under the header. See Message and collaborate.

When a Bot prepares an email or SlackAdd Slack to Grok Bot, in a new tab message, the conversation can show a draft you can edit. Choose Send or Discard.

## Use Siri, Shortcuts, and Live Activities on iPhone

Grok Bot adds shortcuts you can run from Siri, Spotlight, or the Shortcuts app: List Bots, Send Message, Start Dictation, and Start Voice Chat. For example, say "Send a message in Grok Bot."

Start Dictation lets you dictate a message to a Bot without opening the app, as long as your iPhone is unlocked. While it runs, a Live Activity on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island shows its progress, with buttons to cancel or send. A voice chat also shows a Live Activity while you're on the line.

On an iPhone with an Action Button, you can press it to talk with a Bot. In your iPhone's Settings, choose Action Button, swipe to Shortcut, and choose Grok Bot > Start Voice Chat. If you don't pick a Bot for the shortcut, Grok Bot asks which one. Press it again while you're on the line to hang up.

## Create Bots and groups

Use the + control on the home screen to choose New Bot or New Group Chat. You can also edit a Bot profile, manage group members, pin or hide a conversation, and delete a Bot.

## Review the computer

Open the computer from a conversation when you need to:

- Watch browser or desktop work
- Take over for a password, two-factor code, or CAPTCHA
- Inspect the current screen
- Hand control back with I'm done

The screen is the same shared computer used by every Bot on your account.

Updating and recovering the computer aren't available on mobile. Use desktop Grok Bot to update or recover it, or to reconnect your phone when the computer won't connect; see The computer cannot be reached.

## Let a Bot use your phone's apps

A Bot can use some apps on your phone when you ask, such as checking your calendar or setting a timer. This works only in your own chat with a Bot you own in the Grok Bot app. It doesn't work in group chats, in other apps such as Slack, or with a Team Bot someone else owns.

On iPhone and Android:

- Calendar: read your events, and add, change, or delete them. New events go in your default calendar unless you name another one. The Bot can't change or delete a repeating event, and it never invites anyone.
- Contacts: look someone up by name for a phone number, email, address, or birthday, or list your contacts when you ask to see them. The Bot only reads your contacts. If you shared only some contacts with Grok Bot, it sees only those.
- Location: read where your phone is right now. The Bot gets a position, not an address or place name, and how precise it is depends on your phone's location settings.
- Alarms: set an alarm or start a timer. An alarm rings once, the next time your phone's clock shows that time, so it can't be set more than 24 hours ahead. A timer runs for u

Attorneys General Jones and Rayfield File Suit Against SpaceX, Parent Company of X, xAI, and Grok, Over Creation and Promotion of Child Exploitation and Non-Consensual Images on Platform
Virginia and Oregon Attorneys General seek accountability for harms and significant new protections for consumers

***Read the full filing here***

RICHMOND, Va. – Today, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones took a significant step in holding operators of X and its AI tool, Grok, accountable for knowingly failing to protect Virginians, while falsely promoting the safety of its platform and AI tool.

In the lawsuit, the Commonwealth of Virginia alleges that SpaceX, the telecommunications and space transportation conglomerate that operates the social network X and its artificial intelligence company, xAI (now called “SpaceX Super Intelligence”), and developed the Grok family of large language models, failed to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent—while simultaneously promoting the safety of the social media platform and AI tool. The Grok-generated content includes non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), other non-consensual sexualized images, and Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM). Today’s suit was filed in collaboration with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who filed a separate but similar action.

“This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” said Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent. This violation is not acceptable.

The company ignored industry-standard safeguards so xAI could distinguish itself in the AI arms race. Grok’s ability to generate sexualized content was leveraged as a promotional opportunity. These exploitations of Virginian’s safety enabled the widespread creation and distribution of sexualized images through Grok’s integration with X.

“SpaceX allowed Grok and the X platform to create, host, and share unacceptable and dangerous content—and in fact knowingly designed a product without the obviously necessary safeguards in place,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material. The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”

In his filing, Attorney General Jones shows that SpaceX and its subsidiaries marketed Grok as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak,” knowing that its video and image generation technology would be used to produce CSAM, non-consensual intimate images of adults and children (NCII), and other sexualized imagery. In fact, X and its subsidiaries created and promoted a “spicy mode” that specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images.

A study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm (“CCDH”) estimated that, between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok created and posted on X approximately three million sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. That’s an average pace of roughly 190 sexualized images per minute, and one sexualized image of a child approximately every 41 seconds. Nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified by CCDH in its study remained publicly accessible in posts on X a week or more after they were identified—and even many of those that were “removed” could still be accessed via separate URLs.

SpaceX and its subsidiaries publicly assured consumers that robust protections were in place to prevent Grok from creating CSAM, NCII, and other sexualized images. In reality, millions of people — including in Oregon and Virginia — were nevertheless exposed to harmful content and the risk that their own images could be manipulated into sexually explicit content without their consent.

“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” added Attorney General Jones. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold big tech accountable when they break the law.”

“Like the other technology companies that we’re holding accountable, xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” added Attorney General Rayfield.

Attorney General Jones’ lawsuit was filed in the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond. Attorney General Rayfield’s lawsuit was filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court.

Published on: November 23, 2026

xAI.description: SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).
xAI.content:
Skip to content

“Sidelining consent”

# States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn

X says every Grok output is screened, but state AGs say Grok is still making CSAM.

On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.

SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).

Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.

Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online.

“Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint said. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.”

## Millions allegedly harmed

Millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—users as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged.

“xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in a press release.

States alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the new feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged.

Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.”

“Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged.

## SpaceX responds

Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the company has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety said that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues users who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police.

“When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety said. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.”

However, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises users how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged.

Nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall, states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled New York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok users, states alleged.

Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.”

In its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect users, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).”

“Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.”

## Grok CSAM, NCII may trigger steep fines

It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.”

As NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026.

“X users were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged.

Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to users.

“Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged.

Although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of users Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. It said that approximately 6.4 million X accounts were linked to geolocations in the state, while the Grok application was downloaded 986,624 times by users with Virginia-based IP addresses.

“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

Ashley Belanger Senior Policy Reporter

Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

# Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes

State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’

State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’

Jess Weatherbed is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.”

“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.”

The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos. In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift. In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors.

xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios. Our testing at the Verge following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however.

Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages.

The X Safety team said in a statement released after the lawsuits were announced that it takes appropriate measures to address users who generate sexual content involving minors:

1 Comment

“The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards. When some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year, we acted promptly to tighten its protections, which are designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people. To stay ahead of this disgusting and indefensible conduct, we keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics. We also implement sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt before an image is generated and check every output after.”
